Welcome from the Head
As Headteacher here at Norbury Manor Primary School, I would like to extend a warm welcome to everyone who accesses this school website.
Our priority is to ensure that our pupils receive an excellent education in a nurturing environment that encourages our pupils to Make Every Moment Count. We are dedicated to continuing to build opportunities for pupils to achieve the highest academic standards; ensuring that they are known well as individuals and that their unique personality, talents and interests are given the opportunities to flourish within and beyond the classroom.
Sonia Potter, Headteacher
Our Vision
Make Every Moment Count!
We aim to achieve excellence in all areas so that our children, regardless of their starting point, are enthusiastic, independent learners who view the world around them with enquiring minds and give them the resources to be ‘learners today and leaders tomorrow.’
We believe that children whose parents are involved and interested in their learning do well. We involve parents in their children’s learning and encourage them to be active members of the school community. Parent communication is organised to encourage wide participation and honest conversation. We expect all parents to support their children’s educational aspirations and achievements.
OFSTED Report
Ofsted February 2023 said, "Leaders and staff ensure that the school motto of ‘make every moment count’ is part of the everyday culture of the school."
Leaders have ensured that pupils study a broad range of subjects. They have detailed what they want pupils to learn in each year group, including the early years.
Our Curriculum
English
At Norbury Manor Primary, we recognise that improved performance at reading, writing and the spoken language will enable our pupils to express their thoughts and ideas more fluently, accurately and purposefully. This will also help them deal more successfully with other curriculum subjects, while enriching their lives beyond school. The teaching and learning of language skills are therefore given a high priority in our school and, where possible, the creative curriculum and IT will be used as tools.
Reading continues to be prioritised for the whole school with independent reading, story time, We Love Reading and reading events continuing to be timetabled. The school library continues to be supported by the year 6 librarians who have added more books to the collection and have helped the younger children return and choose a book. They also helped to establish a new library software system.
The children continue to use Reading Eggs so they have further access to reading texts at home, as well as reading and spelling homework for all year groups...
To find out more about how we deliver English and to see the whole school curriculum click here
Maths
At Norbury Manor Primary School, we recognise Mathematics as a fundamental pillar in developing confident, independent learners who embody our motto: “Learners today, leaders tomorrow, make every moment count!” Mathematics is essential not only as a core academic discipline but also as a vital life skill that empowers pupils to think critically, solve problems, and engage with the world around them. Rooted in our school values of resilience, scholarship, and excellence, our Mathematics curriculum is designed to foster a deep understanding of numerical concepts, fluency, reasoning, and problem-solving skills, ensuring every pupil—regardless of their starting point or background—can access ambitious learning and achieve their full potential.
Our curriculum is carefully sequenced to build complexity and depth over time, following the principle of “Depth to Enable Breadth.” In Early Years and Key Stage 1, pupils focus on developing core number skills, counting, and early problem-solving, supported by systematic, high-quality phonics-like approaches to mathematical language. In Key Stage 2, learning extends to more complex calculations, reasoning, and application across diverse mathematical domains. Teachers use formative assessment and retrieval practice to identify misconceptions and revisit key concepts, ensuring secure retention and progression. Adaptations and scaffolding are embedded to meet the diverse needs of our pupils, including those with SEND and EAL, supported by ongoing professional development and exemplifications that model best practice and consistency in teaching.
To find out more about how we deliver mathamatics and to see the whole school curriculum click here
Science
At Norbury Manor Primary School, science is a vital pillar of our curriculum, inspiring curiosity, enquiry, and critical thinking in our pupils. Aligned with our school motto, “Learners today, leaders tomorrow, make every moment count!”, our science curriculum nurtures resilient, empathetic, and scholarly learners who view the world through the lens of investigation and discovery. Rooted in our ethos of depth before breadth, science education here empowers pupils to develop a strong foundation of scientific knowledge and skills, fostering a lifelong passion for learning and enabling them to become confident, inquisitive scientists prepared for future academic and life challenges.
Pupils will acquire a rich body of scientific knowledge spanning biology, chemistry, physics, and earth sciences, following the Rising Stars Science Scheme.
Learning in science at Norbury Manor is carefully planned to build increasingly complex mental models over time. Pupils revisit core concepts through varied examples and practical investigations, developing fluency and confidence in applying scientific knowledge.
To see the whole school curriculum click here
Languages
Languages
Norbury Manor primary school ] intends to use the Language Angels scheme of work and resources to ensure we offer a relevant, broad, vibrant and ambitious foreign languages curriculum that will inspire and excite our pupils using a wide variety of topics and themes. All pupils will be expected to achieve their full potential by encouraging high expectations and excellent standards in their foreign language learning - the ultimate aim being that pupils will feel willing and able to continue studying languages beyond key stage 2
The intent is that all content will be continuously updated and reviewed annually, creating a dynamic programme of study that will be clearly outlined in both long-term and short-term planning. This will ensure that the foreign language knowledge of our pupils progresses within each academic year and is extended year upon year throughout the primary phase and, in so doing, will always be relevant and in line with meeting or exceeding national DfE requirements.
The four key language learning skills; listening, speaking, reading and writing will be taught and all necessary grammar will be covered in an age-appropriate way across the primary phase. This will enable pupils to use and apply their learning in a variety of contexts, laying down solid foundations for future language learning and also helping the children improve overall attainment in other subject areas. In addition, the children will be taught how to look up and research language they are unsure of and they w ill have a bank of reference materials to help them with their spoken and written tasks going forward. This bank of reference materials will develop into a reference library to help pupils recall and build on previous knowledge throughout their primary school language learning journey
The intent is that all pupils will develop a genuine interest and positive curiosity about foreign languages, finding them enjoyable and stimulating. Learning a second language will also offer pupils the opportunity to explore relationships between language and identity, develop a deeper understanding of other cultures and the world around them with a better awareness of self, others and cultural differences. The intention is that they will be working towards becoming life-long language learners.
To see the whole school curriculum click here
Humanities
Humanities
At Norbury Manor Primary School, history is a vital subject that connects our pupils to the past, helping them understand the world they live in today and inspiring them to become informed, active citizens of tomorrow. Rooted in our school motto, “Learners today, leaders tomorrow, make every moment count!”, our history curriculum reflects our commitment to resilience, empathy, scholarship, peace, excellence, community, and thankfulness. It is designed to nurture enquiring minds, build strong character, and develop critical thinking, enabling pupils to appreciate diverse cultures, histories, and perspectives within our richly varied school community and beyond.
From Key Stage 1 to Key Stage 2, the history curriculum is carefully sequenced to revisit big ideas and build increasingly complex mental models. Pupils start with fundamental concepts of family, community, and local history, progressing to wider historical perspectives and more sophisticated historical enquiry. Through repeated exposure to key themes and concepts, pupils consolidate their understanding and develop confidence in historical thinking. Teachers use formative assessment and retrieval practice to identify misconceptions and secure mastery, ensuring all pupils meet age-related expectations and are challenged to achieve greater depth.
To see the whole school curriculum click here
At Norbury Manor Primary School, our Geography curriculum is a vital part of our commitment to nurturing curious, resilient, and empathetic learners who are prepared to become informed and active citizens of the 21st century. Rooted in our school motto, “Learners today, leaders tomorrow, make every moment count!”, Geography inspires pupils to explore and understand the diverse world around them, fostering a lifelong fascination with people, places, environments, and the processes that shape our planet. This subject not only enriches pupils’ knowledge but also supports their spiritual, moral, social, and cultural development, aligning with our values of empathy, scholarship, and community.
Our key aims in teaching Geography are to develop pupils’ knowledge of physical and human geography, equip them with essential investigative and critical thinking skills, and encourage them to make meaningful connections between local, national, and global contexts. We strive to ensure every pupil, regardless of background or starting point, masters foundational geographical concepts before progressing to more complex ideas, reflecting our ethos of depth before breadth. Through a carefully sequenced and coherent curriculum, pupils will build knowledge that is transferable across subjects, enhancing their literacy and numeracy skills and supporting their wider academic success.
To see the whole school curriculum click here
Art & Design Technology
Art & Design Technology
To ensure all pupils produce creative, imaginative work. Children have the opportunity to explore their ideas and record their experiences, as well as exploring the work of others and evaluate different creative ideas. Children will become confident and proficient in a variety of techniques including drawing, painting, sculpting, as well as other selected craft skills, e.g. collage, printing, weaving and patterns. Children will also develop their knowledge of famous artists, designers and craft makers. Children will also develop their interest and curiosity about art and design through a series of lessons offering skills progression, knowledge progression and offering children the opportunity to ask questions and demonstrate their skills in a variety of ways. The lessons will offer the chance for children to develop their emotional expression through art to further enhance their personal, social and emotional development. This progression grid can support any subject leader or teacher of art to ensure progression of skills and knowledge
PlanIt Design and Technology aims to inspire children through a broad range of practical experiences to create innovative designs which solve real and relevant problems within a variety of different contexts. The iterative design process is fundamental and runs throughout the PlanIt units. This iterative process encourages children to identify real and relevant problems, critically evaluate existing products and then take risks and innovate when designing and creating solutions to the problems. As part of the iterative process, time is built in to reflect, evaluate and improve on prototypes using design criteria throughout to support this process. Opportunities are provided for children to evaluate key events and individuals who have helped shape the world, showing the real impact of design and technology on the wider environment and helping to inspire children to become the next generation of innovators.
To see the whole school curriculum click here
Music
Music
Through the musical programme Charanga, the children develop their understanding, make musical judgements, apply their new learning, develop their aural memory, express themselves physically, emotionally and through discussion and create their own musical ideas.
Performing vocally and with instruments is central to the programme. Children are also given the opportunity to perform during class assemblies, productions, challenge week and the school choir.
The choir perform in assemblies, at school functions and other events in the local area. Our choir has performed at the Trinity College choir event.
To see the whole school curriculum click here
Computing
Computing
Our computing curriculum has been developed to support children to become proficient users of technology so that they develop the knowledge and skills to thrive in the ever-changing technological world. It is in-line with National Curriculum guidelines and includes coding.
Norbury Manor follow the ‘Switched on Computing’ programme.

Fundamental British Values
Preparing our pupils for life in modern Britain
At Norbury Manor Primary School, we actively promote the fundamental British values of:
Democracy • The Rule of Law • Individual Liberty • Mutual Respect and Tolerance of Those with Different Faiths and Beliefs
These values are an important part of preparing our pupils for life in modern Britain. They help children understand their rights and responsibilities, respect others, make informed choices and recognise the important role they can play within their school, local community and wider society. Schools are expected to actively promote these values as part of pupils' wider development
At Norbury Manor, British values are not taught as a stand-alone topic. They are embedded throughout school life: through our curriculum, assemblies, RESPECT values, Skills Builder programme, behaviour expectations, pupil leadership, enrichment opportunities and the relationships we build with one another.
Our diverse school community gives our children valuable opportunities to learn with and from people with different languages, cultures, experiences, faiths and beliefs. We want every pupil to feel that they belong, that their voice matters and that they have a responsibility to ensure others feel the same.
Democracy – having a voice and making a difference
We teach pupils that democracy is about people having a voice, listening to different viewpoints and participating responsibly in decisions.
Children experience democracy directly through our School Council. Representatives are elected by their classmates and are expected to listen to the views of the pupils they represent and bring these to council meetings.
Our pupil leadership opportunities enable children to understand that leadership involves service, responsibility, listening and action, rather than simply holding a title.
Pupils have opportunities to:
discuss issues with school leaders and governors;
represent the views of their classmates;
The Rule of Law – understanding rights, rules and responsibilities
Children learn that communities need agreed rules and laws to protect people's rights, keep people safe and ensure that people are treated fairly.
Our school expectations and behaviour systems help pupils understand that their actions have consequences and that everyone has responsibilities towards others.
Through our curriculum, assemblies and everyday school life, pupils learn:
why we have rules and laws;
Visits and engagement with organisations and people serving our community, including the police, fire service and civic leaders, help children understand how laws, public services and civic responsibilities operate beyond school
the difference between right and wrong;
that rules apply to everyone;
that rights come with responsibilities;
how choices can affect other people; and
Individual Liberty – making safe and informed choices
At Norbury Manor, pupils are encouraged to become confident, independent learners who can make choices while understanding their responsibilities towards themselves and others.
Children are taught that individual liberty includes the freedom to express ideas, develop interests and hold beliefs, while recognising that these freedoms exist within the law and must respect the rights and freedoms of other people.
We provide opportunities for pupils to make choices about their learning, take on responsibilities, participate in enrichment and leadership activities and express their views.
Through PSHE, Relationships and Health Education, online safety, safeguarding and the wider curriculum, pupils also learn how to:
make informed and age-appropriate choices;
recognise unsafe or unhealthy situations;
understand personal boundaries;
seek help when they need it;
use technology safely and responsibly;
develop confidence and independence; and
Mutual Respect and Tolerance of Different Faiths and Beliefs
Respect is at the heart of Norbury Manor.
Our school community includes families from a wide range of cultures, languages, faiths, beliefs and backgrounds. We see this diversity as an important part of children's education and preparation for life in modern Britain.
We teach pupils that people may have different beliefs, traditions, cultures, families and viewpoints and that difference should be approached with curiosity, empathy and respect, not prejudice or discrimination.
This is promoted through:
Pupils learn that people have the legal freedom to hold different faiths and beliefs, including having no religious belief, and that differences should never be a reason for discriminatory or prejudicial behaviour. GOV.UK
our RESPECT values and weekly RESPECT assemblies;
Religious Education;
PSHE and Relationships Education;
English, History, Geography and the wider curriculum;
discussion of stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination; and
British Values, RESPECT and Skills Builder
Our approach to British values is strengthened by our RESPECT values and Skills Builder programme.
Children do not simply learn the vocabulary of democracy, liberty, law and respect. They develop the skills they need to put these principles into practice: speaking, listening, teamwork, leadership, problem solving, creativity, staying positive and aiming high.
For example, pupils need speaking and listening skills to participate in democratic discussions; leadership and teamwork to contribute to their community; empathy to understand perspectives different from their own; and problem-solving skills to resolve disagreements constructively.
Our Monday RESPECT Assemblies, class discussions and wider curriculum give pupils regular opportunities to consider values, behaviours, rights and responsibilities and how these apply to real-life situations.
Pupil Leadership and Active Citizenship
We want pupils to recognise that they can make a positive contribution now, not simply when they become adults.
Leadership opportunities across the school include our School Council, pupil ambassadors, class responsibilities and opportunities for pupils to lead activities and contribute to assemblies.
These experiences help pupils learn to listen to others, take responsibility, work collaboratively, represent their peers and contribute positively to their school and community.
Challenging Discrimination, Extremism and Radicalisation
Actively promoting British values also means that we challenge prejudice, discrimination and behaviours or views that undermine these values, in an age-appropriate way. GOV.UK
We encourage pupils to ask questions, think critically, consider evidence and discuss different viewpoints respectfully. Where political or controversial issues are explored, pupils are supported to understand that different views may exist and are given the knowledge and context needed to consider them appropriately. GOV.UK
Our work to promote British values also forms part of our safeguarding responsibilities under the Prevent duty. Prevent is approached as a safeguarding responsibility: its purpose in education is to identify and support individuals who may be susceptible to radicalisation before risks escalate. GOV.UK
Staff receive appropriate safeguarding training and know how to respond if they have concerns about a child. The current Ofsted inspection toolkit expects schools to fulfil their statutory safeguarding responsibilities, including the Prevent duty.
Working Together
Promoting British values is a shared responsibility between pupils, staff, parents and carers, governors and our wider community.
Through our curriculum and the everyday life of our school, we aim to develop pupils who are confident, respectful, responsible and compassionate; who can think for themselves, listen to others and make a positive contribution to modern Britain.
Our ambition reflects our school motto:
“Leaders today, learners tomorrow – make every moment count.”
For further information for families about protecting children from extremism and radicalisation, visit Educate Against Hate.
You can also read the government's current Prevent duty guidance for education settings.

Vision, Ethos, and Values
Learners Today. Leaders Tomorrow. Make Every Moment Count!
Our Vision
At Norbury Manor Primary School, our vision is for every child, regardless of their starting point, to become a confident, enthusiastic, and independent learner who is prepared for the opportunities and challenges of the future.
We have high expectations for every pupil. We aim to develop the knowledge, skills, character, and confidence children need to achieve academically, contribute positively to their community, and become learners today and leaders tomorrow.
Our Ethos
Norbury Manor is a nurturing, inclusive, and ambitious school where every child is known, valued, and encouraged to succeed. We believe that children thrive when they feel safe, develop a strong sense of belonging, and are challenged to achieve their best.
Our ethos is built around high expectations, positive relationships, and respect for ourselves, each other, and our community. We celebrate the diversity of our school and ensure that individual needs, backgrounds, languages, cultures, and beliefs are recognised and valued. We promote the fundamental British Values of democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, mutual respect and tolerance of those of different faiths and beliefs, preparing pupils to participate positively in life in modern Britain.
We believe education is a partnership. We work closely with parents and carers and encourage families to take an active role in their children's learning and wider school life.
Our RESPECT Values
Our RESPECT values underpin our ethos and permeate all areas of school life:
R – ResilienceE – EmpathyS – ScholarshipP – PeaceE – ExcellenceC – CommunityT – Thankfulness
Our values are brought to life through our Skills Builder approach, helping children understand not only what our values mean, but the skills and behaviours that enable them to demonstrate those values every day. Each RESPECT value is linked to essential skills and the fundamental British Values, supporting pupils to become confident, responsible and respectful members of their school and wider community.
These values and skills are reinforced through ClassDojo, where pupils are recognised for demonstrating them through their everyday learning, behaviour and interactions with others.

Our Tree of Learning
Our Tree of Learning represents how children grow and develop throughout their time at Norbury Manor.
The roots represent the essential values, skills and foundations that enable our pupils to grow. The trunk represents the strength of character, knowledge and experiences they develop, while the branches and leaves represent the knowledge, ideas and concepts they acquire as they progress through school.
Just as a tree continues to grow and change, we want our pupils to continually develop their knowledge, deepen their understanding, challenge their thinking and build the skills they need for their future.

As Headteacher of Norbury Manor Primary School, I am delighted to welcome you to our school website.
Our priority is to ensure that every pupil receives an excellent education in a nurturing, inclusive and ambitious environment. We have high expectations for all our children while ensuring they are known and valued as individuals, with opportunities for their unique talents, interests and personalities to flourish.

We are proud of our diverse and inclusive school community and value the strong partnerships we build with our families. I hope our website gives you a flavour of life at Norbury Manor, and we warmly welcome you to visit and experience our school for yourself.

Phonics & Early Reading
Learning to Read at Norbury Manor
At Norbury Manor Primary School, we want every child to develop the skills, confidence and enjoyment needed to become a fluent and successful reader.
We use Read Write Inc. Phonics (RWI) to support the systematic teaching of early reading. Children are taught to recognise sounds, blend them together to read words and develop increasing accuracy and fluency.
Children progress through the programme according to their developing phonics knowledge and reading skills. Regular assessment helps staff identify what children have secured and where additional teaching or practice is needed.
The videos and guidance on this page have been provided to help parents and carers understand how phonics is taught at Norbury Manor and use the same approaches when supporting reading at home.
What is Phonics?
Phonics teaches children the relationship between spoken sounds and the letters or groups of letters used to represent them.
Children learn that letters and groups of letters represent sounds. They then learn to blend these sounds together to read words.
Developing secure phonics knowledge helps children become increasingly independent readers and provides important foundations for spelling and writing.
This video provides an introduction to phonics and explains how learning sounds helps children begin to read
Saying the Sounds Correctly
How we pronounce sounds is important when children are learning to blend.
Children are taught to say sounds clearly. Using the same pronunciation at home and at school makes it easier for children to recognise sounds and blend them successfully when reading.
Use this video to hear how the sounds are pronounced so that you can practise them with your child at home.
Learning to Blend
Once children begin recognising sounds, they learn to blend sounds together to read words.
In Read Write Inc., children learn to use Fred Talk. Fred can only speak in sounds, so children hear the individual sounds and blend them together to make the whole word.
With regular practice, children become quicker at recognising and blending sounds until they are increasingly able to read words automatically.
This video demonstrates how children are taught to blend sounds when reading.
How We Group Children for Phonics
Children develop their phonics knowledge at different rates. We therefore regularly assess children's phonics and reading so that teaching can respond to what they need to learn next.
Children may work in Read Write Inc. groups based on their current stage of phonics development rather than simply their age or class.
Groups are reviewed regularly as children develop their knowledge and become increasingly fluent readers.
This video explains how our Read Write Inc. sound groups work at Norbury Manor and how they support children's progress.
Moving on to More Complex Sounds

What is Phonics?

Children learn that letters and groups of letters represent sounds. They then learn to blend these sounds together to read words.
Developing secure phonics knowledge helps children become increasingly independent readers and provides important foundations for spelling and writing.

Early Years Curriculum
Building Strong Foundations for Learning
At Norbury Manor Primary School, our Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) includes children in Nursery and Reception.
We believe that the early years provide the foundations for children's future learning and development. Our curriculum provides children with a balance of carefully planned teaching, purposeful play, exploration and practical experiences that encourage them to become confident, curious and increasingly independent learners.
We recognise that children enter the Early Years with different experiences, strengths and starting points. Our curriculum is therefore designed to be ambitious, inclusive and responsive to individual needs, while ensuring that every child has opportunities to develop the knowledge, language and skills they need for the next stage of their education.
The Four Principles of the EYFS
Our Early Years provision is shaped by the four guiding principles of the Early Years Foundation Stage.
A Unique Child
Every child is unique. We want children to become resilient, capable, confident and self-assured learners.
We recognise children's individual starting points, interests and needs and provide appropriate challenge and support to enable them to make progress.
Positive Relationships
Children learn to be strong and independent through positive, secure and caring relationships.
We value close partnerships between children, parents and carers, key people and the wider school community. These relationships help children feel safe, valued and ready to learn.
Enabling Environments
Children learn and develop well within stimulating and well-organised environments that respond to their interests and needs.
Our indoor and outdoor learning environments provide opportunities for children to explore, investigate, communicate, create, solve problems and develop independence.
Learning and Development
Children develop and learn in different ways and at different rates.
Our practitioners carefully consider what children already know and can do and use this information to plan appropriate teaching, experiences, interactions and opportunities for purposeful play.
How Children Learn
Young children learn through a combination of direct teaching, adult interaction, purposeful play, exploration and first-hand experiences.
Our adults play an important role in children's learning. They model language and skills, introduce new knowledge and vocabulary, ask questions, demonstrate, provide appropriate support and recognise opportunities to extend children's thinking.
Children are also given time and opportunities to explore ideas, practise what they have learned and develop independence.
Characteristics of Effective Teaching and Learning
The EYFS identifies three characteristics that describe how children engage with their learning:
Playing and Exploring – EngagementChildren investigate and experience things and are encouraged to have a go.
Active Learning – MotivationChildren develop concentration, keep trying when they encounter difficulties and enjoy achieving what they set out to do.
Creating and Thinking Critically – ThinkingChildren develop their own ideas, make connections between ideas and develop strategies for doing things.
These characteristics help children develop the confidence, curiosity and independence that support learning throughout school.
The Seven Areas of Learning and Development
The EYFS curriculum is organised into seven interconnected areas of learning and development.
Three are known as the Prime Areas because they provide particularly important foundations for children's learning and development.
Prime Areas
Communication and Language
Children develop their ability to listen, understand and communicate.
Through conversations, stories, songs, rhymes, role play and interactions with adults and other children, they develop their vocabulary and confidence in expressing ideas.
Personal, Social and Emotional Development
Children learn to understand themselves and others, build positive relationships and manage their emotions and behaviour.
They develop confidence, independence, resilience and an understanding of how to keep themselves healthy and safe.
Our Early Years provision also begins children's journey with our RESPECT values and Skills Builder essential skills.
Physical Development
Children develop their gross and fine motor skills, coordination, strength and control through a wide range of indoor and outdoor experiences.
They also develop the physical skills needed for increasing independence, including the foundations required for writing.
Specific Areas
The four Specific Areas build upon the foundations developed through the Prime Areas.
Literacy
Children develop a love of stories, books, rhymes and language while beginning to become readers and writers.
In Reception, our systematic approach to early reading is supported by Read Write Inc. Phonics.
Mathematics
Children develop a secure foundation in number and numerical patterns through practical experiences, mathematical talk, exploration and carefully planned teaching.
Children learn to notice patterns and relationships, compare quantities, develop their understanding of number and use mathematical ideas within meaningful situations.
Understanding the World
Children develop their knowledge and understanding of the physical world and their community.
They explore the natural world, learn about people and communities, notice similarities and differences, explore the past and begin developing their understanding of the wider world.
Expressive Arts and Design
Children have opportunities to imagine, create and express themselves through art, music, movement, dance, role play and imaginative experiences.
They explore different materials, techniques and ways of representing their ideas.
Learning Through Our Environment
Our Early Years environment is an important part of the curriculum.
Children have opportunities to learn through both indoor and outdoor provision, with carefully selected resources and experiences designed to promote communication, exploration, creativity, physical development, problem solving and independence.
Adults enhance children's learning by introducing new vocabulary, modelling, questioning and helping children make connections between their experiences and the knowledge being taught.
The environment provides opportunities for children to revisit, practise and apply their learning in different contexts.
An Inclusive Early Years
We want every child to participate, belong and succeed.
Children arrive in our Early Years with different experiences and at different stages of development. Practitioners observe and assess children's learning so that teaching, interactions, resources and support can be adapted appropriately.
For children who speak English as an additional language, we value and recognise their home languages while providing rich opportunities to develop their understanding and use of English.
Children with SEND or emerging additional needs are supported through early identification, appropriate adaptations and close partnership with families and other professionals where required.
Our expectations remain ambitious while recognising that children may need different routes and different levels of support to achieve success.
Assessment in the Early Years
Assessment is an ongoing part of teaching and learning.
Practitioners build their understanding of children through observation, interaction, discussion and children's responses during adult-led and child-initiated learning.
This helps adults understand what children know and can do, identify their next steps and adapt provision accordingly.
Assessment should support children's learning rather than interrupt it, so much of our assessment happens naturally as adults talk, play, teach and interact with children.
In Reception, children's learning and development is considered against the Early Learning Goals at the end of the EYFS.
Preparing for the Next Stage
Throughout Nursery and Reception, we progressively build the knowledge, language, skills, independence and learning behaviours children need to be successful as they move through school.
Our Early Years curriculum is the beginning of the Norbury Manor curriculum journey, rather than a separate experience from the rest of the school.
Children begin developing our RESPECT values and Skills Builder essential skills, learn how to work with others, communicate their ideas, solve problems, persevere and become increasingly independent learners.
Explore What We Teach
For further information about what children learn throughout Nursery and Reception, please visit our Curriculum Maps page.
For further information about our Early Years provision, please contact the school office, who will direct your enquiry to the appropriate member of staff.

Nurture at Norbury Manor Primary School
Achieve • Belong • Thrive
At Norbury Manor Primary School, nurture is part of our whole-school approach to inclusion. We want every child to feel safe, valued and understood so that they are ready to learn, build positive relationships and participate fully in school life.
We recognise that children's readiness to learn can be affected by their social and emotional development, communication, relationships, experiences and ability to regulate their emotions. Nurture helps us identify and reduce these barriers while maintaining high expectations for every child.
Our targeted nurture provision is called The NMP Nest. It provides planned, short-term support for pupils whose social, emotional, communication or regulation needs are creating barriers to learning, participation or wellbeing.
The Nest is not a punishment, a time-out room or an alternative to the classroom. It forms part of our graduated approach to supporting pupils and is designed to help children develop skills that they can increasingly use independently in their classroom, on the playground and throughout the wider school day.
Our approach reflects the current national emphasis on identifying needs early and providing high-quality, adaptive and inclusive support within mainstream schools.
Explore Nurture at NMP
The Six Principles of Nurture
Our practice is guided by the Six Principles of Nurture. These principles help us understand children's development, relationships, communication, behaviour and wellbeing. NurtureUK – The Six Principles of Nurture
1. Children's learning is understood developmentally
NMP pupil language: “We learn in our own way and in our own time.”
Children develop socially, emotionally and academically at different rates. We consider what a child can currently understand and manage and provide appropriate support and challenge from that starting point. Developmental understanding does not mean lowering expectations; it means providing the right scaffolding to help each child progress.
NMP Value: Excellence
2. The classroom offers a safe base
NMP pupil language: “Our school is a safe place to be.”
Children learn best when they feel physically and emotionally safe. Predictable routines, clear boundaries and calm, consistent adults help children develop trust and confidence. Our nurture spaces provide a secure base while remaining connected to children's classrooms and the wider life of the school.
NMP Value: Community
3. Nurture is important for the development of wellbeing
NMP pupil language: “We believe in ourselves and look after our wellbeing.”
Positive relationships are central to nurture. Adults notice effort, recognise small steps of progress and create opportunities for children to experience success. We help children develop confidence, resilience, self-esteem and a strong sense of belonging.
NMP Value: Scholarship
4. Language is a vital means of communication
NMP pupil language: “We use our words to talk about how we feel.”
Children need language to understand and communicate their thoughts, feelings and needs. Adults model appropriate emotional vocabulary and create regular opportunities for conversation, reflection, problem-solving and listening. Visuals, signing and other communication approaches are used where appropriate to ensure communication is accessible.
5. All behaviour is communication
NMP pupil language: “Our behaviour can show how we are feeling.”
We recognise that behaviour can communicate an underlying emotion, difficulty or unmet need. Adults seek to understand what a child may be communicating while maintaining clear, safe and consistent expectations.
Understanding behaviour does not mean accepting unsafe or inappropriate behaviour. Instead, we teach children the skills and strategies they need to communicate, regulate and make increasingly positive choices.
6. Transitions are significant in children's lives
NMP pupil language: “We can cope with changes in our lives.”
Changes can be particularly difficult for some children. We carefully support transitions between activities, classrooms, adults, year groups and schools. Children may use visual timetables, advance warnings, familiar routines, trusted adults and transition activities to help them manage change successfully.
NMP Values: Resilience and Thankfulness
These are the current six principles used by NurtureUK, which emphasises predictable routines, emotionally available adults, wellbeing, communication, understanding behaviour and planned transitions. nurtureuk
The NMP Nest
The NMP Nest is our targeted nurture provision within our wider inclusive school approach.
It supports children to:
Children normally attend two planned afternoon sessions each week. They remain members of their mainstream class and continue to access an ambitious curriculum.
The purpose of The Nest is transfer, not dependence. Success is not simply a child managing well while they are in the nurture space. We want children to use the skills and strategies they develop successfully in their classroom, on the playground and throughout everyday school life.
Our Nurture Environment
Our dedicated nurture spaces include Willow Hub and the Maple Hub space in Blossom House. …
Our nurture environments are designed to be calm, welcoming, predictable and accessible. Children experience consistent routines and trusted adults alongside spaces and resources that support learning, communication, play, social interaction and emotional regulation.
The environment may include opportunities for shared activities, practical learning, sensory or regulation activities, conversation, group work and quiet reflection.
The physical environment is only one part of a safe base. Just as important are the relationships, routines and adult responses that help children know what to expect and feel secure.
Teaching and Learning in The Nest
Children attending The Nest continue to be part of the wider NMP curriculum.
The Nest curriculum provides practical, social and curriculum-linked experiences through which children can practise communication, cooperation, emotional regulation, resilience and independence. The programme is deliberately connected to our wider curriculum rather than operating as a separate curriculum.
Learning may include:
Each half term also provides opportunities to explicitly teach and revisit one of the Six Principles of Nurture and connect it to our NMP values.
Sessions have clear routines but remain responsive to the developmental needs and individual outcomes of the pupils attending.
PSHE and social and emotional learning
emotional literacy and regulation
communication and language
collaborative games and activities
practical STEM and Design Technology
physical activity and cooperative games
Natural Norbury and outdoor learning

preparation for change and transition.
How Children Are Identified for The Nest
Placement in The Nest is based on a child's identified barriers and developmental needs. It is not determined by a diagnosis, attainment level, one Boxall Profile score or a single behaviour incident.
We build a rounded picture of the child using information that may include teacher assessment, the Boxall Profile, pupil voice, parent/carer views, SEND information, attendance or behaviour information where relevant, previous interventions and advice from other professionals.
The Nurture Team, SENCO and Headteacher consider the evidence and agree the most appropriate support. Parents and carers are consulted before a child begins attending The Nest.
This reflects the school's Assess – Plan – Do – Review approach and our commitment to identifying and meeting needs as early as possible.
Working with Children and Families
Children and their families are important partners in nurture.
We listen to children's views about what they find difficult, what helps them and what they would like adults to understand. Parents and carers bring invaluable knowledge about their child and contribute information about strengths, concerns, successful strategies and priorities.
Class teachers remain responsible for children's education, progress and wellbeing while they attend The Nest. Nest staff and class staff work together so that successful strategies are used consistently across the school day.
That child-centred approach is also consistent with current statutory safeguarding guidance, which says children's wishes and feelings should be sought, heard and responded to and that practitioners should work with children, families and those who know them well.
Assessing Progress and Impact
Assessment helps us understand children's needs, plan appropriate support and determine whether nurture is making a meaningful difference.
We do not rely upon a single measure. Evidence may include the Boxall Profile, teacher assessment, pupil voice, parent/carer views, individual nurture outcomes, classroom observations and relevant information about learning, attendance, behaviour or SEND.
Children usually have two or three specific developmental outcomes, which are reviewed during their time in The Nest.
We look for changes such as improved emotional vocabulary, greater independence, stronger relationships, increased engagement in learning, improved regulation, greater resilience and a stronger sense of belonging.
Most importantly, we look for evidence that children are increasingly able to use these skills independently in everyday school life.
Reintegration, Step-Down and Exit
The aim of nurture is not for children to remain indefinitely in targeted provision.
Planning for successful reintegration begins when a child enters The Nest. Strategies that work successfully are shared with classroom staff and deliberately transferred into everyday school life.
Progress is regularly reviewed using the child's Boxall Profile, individual outcomes, teacher evidence, pupil voice, parent/carer views and evidence of how successfully skills are transferring beyond The Nest.
Depending on need and progress, the outcome may be to continue provision, adapt the child's targets, begin a gradual step-down or exit The Nest.
Where a child is ready to leave, this is carefully planned. Attendance may reduce gradually, successful strategies continue in class, and progress is followed up to ensure that improvements are sustained.
Nurture Across NMP
Nurture at Norbury Manor is much bigger than The Nest.
The Six Principles of Nurture underpin our wider approach to relationships, behaviour, inclusion and pastoral care. Adults across the school use predictable routines, calm and consistent responses, emotionally available relationships and appropriate language to help children understand and communicate their needs.
This means that children do not have to be part of The Nest to benefit from a nurturing approach.
Every child should be supported to Achieve, Belong and Thrive.

Relationships and Health Education
At Norbury Manor Primary School, we want every child to develop the knowledge, skills and confidence they need to build positive relationships, keep themselves safe, look after their physical and mental health and prepare for life in modern Britain.
Relationships Education and Health Education form an important part of our wider Personal, Social, Health and Economic (PSHE) curriculum and complement our work on safeguarding, wellbeing, behaviour, online safety and personal development.
Our teaching is inclusive and age-appropriate and takes account of the needs and maturity of our pupils and our diverse school community.
What are schools required to teach?
Relationships Education is compulsory in all primary schools and Health Education is compulsory in state-funded primary schools. The Department for Education's revised statutory guidance came into effect on 1 September 2026.
At primary school, Relationships Education establishes the foundations children need to develop positive and safe relationships. This includes learning about families and people who care for us, caring friendships, respectful relationships, online relationships and being safe.
Health Education helps children develop their understanding of physical health and mental wellbeing, including how they can make decisions that support their own health and safety.
Our curriculum is designed so that this learning develops progressively as children move through the school.
At Norbury Manor, we provide age-appropriate teaching that helps pupils understand growing up, relationships, their bodies and the changes they will experience as they mature.
This learning is approached sensitively and factually, with consideration given to pupils' age, maturity and individual needs.
The Right to Withdraw
It is important that parents understand the distinction between Relationships Education, Health Education, Science and Sex Education.
Parents cannot withdraw their child from Relationships Education or Health Education.
There is also no right to withdraw from the National Curriculum for Science, including statutory content relating to areas such as the human body, growth, puberty and reproduction in plants and animals.
Parents do have the right to request that their child is withdrawn from sex education taught outside the National Curriculum for Science in a primary school.
Relationships and Sex Education at NMP
Sex education is not compulsory in primary schools. However, the Department for Education recommends that primary schools provide age-appropriate sex education, particularly in Years 5 and/or 6, alongside relevant learning within the National Curriculum for Science.
Working in Partnership with Parents and Carers
Parents and carers are children's first educators, and we recognise the importance of working in partnership with families when teaching Relationships and Sex Education.
The DfE expects primary schools to consult parents about sex education content and to support parents in talking to their children about this learning.
Our curriculum and policy are therefore reviewed with consideration given to:
Our teaching is designed to be factual, sensitive, inclusive and appropriate to children's developmental stage.
pupils' age, maturity and learning needs;
the needs of pupils with SEND;
physical and emotional development;
online as well as offline relationships; and
Creating a Safe Environment for Learning
Relationships and health education sometimes involves sensitive subjects. We therefore establish clear expectations so that children know that lessons are a safe and respectful place to learn.
Teachers use age-appropriate language and carefully selected resources. Pupils are encouraged to ask questions, listen respectfully to different views and understand that they do not have to share personal experiences in front of their peers.
Where a pupil's question indicates a possible safeguarding concern, staff follow the school's safeguarding procedures.
How This Fits with Our Wider Curriculum
Relationships and Health Education does not sit in isolation.
Children encounter and apply this learning throughout school life through PSHE, Science, Computing and online safety, PE, assemblies, our RESPECT values, Skills Builder, nurture provision and safeguarding education.
This helps children make connections between what they learn in a lesson and the decisions and relationships they encounter in everyday life.
Our aim is for pupils to leave Norbury Manor increasingly able to:
develop healthy and respectful relationships; understand and manage their emotions; recognise when something is unsafe; know how and where to ask for help; make informed choices about their health and wellbeing; respect themselves and others; and approach growing up with knowledge and confidence.

Our Curriculum Subjects
At Norbury Manor Primary School, we provide an ambitious, broad and balanced curriculum from the Early Years through to Year 6.
Our curriculum is carefully sequenced so that children build their knowledge, vocabulary, understanding and skills over time. New learning connects to what children already know, while opportunities to revisit, retrieve and apply important knowledge help children develop increasingly secure understanding.
We have high expectations for all pupils. Teaching is adapted and appropriate support is provided so that children with different starting points and needs can successfully access and participate in our curriculum.
The programmes and schemes referenced on this page are resources that support the delivery of the Norbury Manor curriculum. Teachers use their professional knowledge of our pupils and the curriculum to select, adapt and supplement these resources where appropriate.
For detailed information about what is taught in each year group, please visit our Curriculum Maps page.
English
Early Reading & Phonics
Our Vision
We want every child to develop the strong foundations in phonics and early reading they need to become a confident and fluent reader.
What Learning Looks Like
We use Read Write Inc. Phonics (RWI) to support the systematic teaching of early reading. Beginning in the Early Years, children learn the sounds represented by letters and groups of letters and how to blend these sounds to read words.
Children read carefully matched, fully decodable books so that they can practise and apply the sounds and words they have been taught. As children become increasingly secure and fluent, they progress into our wider reading curriculum.
How We Know Children Are Learning
Children's phonics and early reading development is assessed regularly. Teachers use assessment to identify what children have secured, provide additional teaching and practice where needed, and ensure children progress when they are ready.
Find out more about our approach, home reading books and how you can support your child on our Phonics page.
Reading
Our Vision
We want every child to become a fluent, confident and thoughtful reader who enjoys reading.
Through reading, children encounter new knowledge, vocabulary, people, places, cultures and ideas. We want children not only to learn to read but to choose to read.
What Learning Looks Like
Once children are ready to move beyond fully decodable texts, they access increasingly challenging books through their classrooms and school library.
Children progressively learn to:
Alongside appropriately challenging reading material, children select Reading for Pleasure books based on their interests.
We also use Reading Eggs and Reading Eggspress as additional digital resources. These provide opportunities for children to practise phonics, vocabulary, fluency and comprehension at school and at home.
read accurately and fluently;
understand and use increasingly sophisticated vocabulary;
retrieve information;
make inferences and justify ideas using evidence;
predict and summarise;
discuss authors' choices;
compare and discuss texts;
express and explain their responses to reading.
How We Know Children Are Learning
Teachers build a picture of children's reading through listening to them read, discussion, questioning, comprehension activities and assessment.
Information from Reading Eggs and Reading Eggspress provides an additional source of assessment information and helps teachers identify children's next steps.
Writing
Our Vision
We want children to become confident, creative and purposeful writers who can communicate their ideas effectively for different audiences and purposes.
Children should leave Norbury Manor able to draw upon secure knowledge of vocabulary, grammar, punctuation, spelling and text structure while developing their own voice as writers.
What Learning Looks Like
Our writing approach has evolved from our experience of Talk for Writing and has been further developed through professional learning, including the DfE curriculum webinars.
High-quality texts provide models of effective writing and introduce children to rich vocabulary, sentence structures and the features of different genres.
Children move through a carefully planned teaching sequence:
Explore and analyse → Learn and practise → Plan → Compose → Revise and edit → Apply independently
Teachers explicitly model writing and provide guided practice before children apply their learning with increasing independence.
Grammar and punctuation are taught explicitly and, wherever appropriate, children are expected to apply this knowledge within meaningful writing.
Children write for different purposes and audiences within English and across the wider curriculum.
How We Know Children Are Learning
Teachers assess children's writing through their independent application of taught knowledge and skills.
Children's writing is considered over time rather than relying upon a single piece of work. Assessment identifies what has become secure and what needs to be taught, practised or applied next.
Spelling
Our Vision
We want children to become increasingly confident spellers who can draw upon their knowledge of sounds, spelling patterns and word structure when writing independently.
What Learning Looks Like
Early spelling develops alongside phonics. As children progress, Read Write Inc. Spelling supports our systematic teaching of spelling.
Children develop their knowledge of:
Children are encouraged to apply their spelling knowledge within their independent writing.
phoneme-grapheme correspondence;
spelling patterns and conventions;
root words and word families;
prefixes and suffixes;
word structure;
strategies for remembering particularly challenging words.
How We Know Children Are Learning
Teachers assess spelling through taught activities and children's independent writing. This enables teachers to identify patterns that have been secured and those requiring further teaching and practice.
Mathematics
Our Vision
We want children to become confident, fluent and successful mathematicians who enjoy mathematics and can use what they know to reason, make connections and solve problems.
We want children to understand mathematics rather than simply remember procedures, while also developing the fluency and automatic recall that allows them to tackle increasingly complex mathematical thinking.
What Learning Looks Like
We have developed our own Spiral Maths curriculum, drawing upon mastery principles and high-quality mathematical resources.
Important mathematical knowledge and concepts are revisited, strengthened and developed over time. This helps children connect new learning with what they already know and gives them repeated opportunities to deepen and apply their understanding.
Our mathematics teaching develops three interconnected areas:
Fluency – developing secure mathematical knowledge, number facts and efficient calculation methods.
Reasoning – explaining mathematical thinking, identifying relationships and patterns, making connections and justifying answers.
Problem Solving – applying mathematical knowledge and selecting appropriate strategies to solve familiar and unfamiliar problems.
Where appropriate, children experience all three within their mathematics learning so that they move beyond simply finding an answer to being able to explain, justify and apply their mathematical thinking.
Our I Do, We Do, You Do approach supports children as they move from explicit teacher modelling and guided practice towards increasingly independent mathematical thinking.
Teachers use practical resources, representations and mathematical images where these help children develop conceptual understanding before moving towards increasingly abstract mathematics.
Multiplication & Times Tables
Secure multiplication knowledge is an important foundation for later mathematics.
Children therefore have dedicated times-table teaching and practice, alongside opportunities to apply multiplication knowledge within their wider mathematics lessons.
We use Times Tables Rock Stars as an additional resource to help children develop the speed, accuracy and automatic recall of multiplication and division facts.
Regular practice helps children build fluency so that recalling multiplication facts places less demand on their thinking when they encounter more complex mathematics.
Assessment – Cold and Hot Tasks
Assessment is an integral part of our mathematics teaching.
At the beginning of a mathematical concept or unit, children complete a Cold Task. This helps teachers establish children's starting points, identify what they already know and uncover gaps or misconceptions.
Teachers use the outcomes to adapt their planning and teaching so that learning responds to the needs of the children.
Following teaching, children complete a Hot Task linked to the same mathematical concept. Teachers use this alongside children's work and their ongoing assessment to evaluate what children have learned and the progress they have made.
The process therefore supports a continuous cycle:
Assess → Identify starting points → Adapt teaching → Teach and practise → Reassess → Identify next steps
Mathletics
Children also have access to Mathletics, which provides additional curriculum-linked opportunities to practise and consolidate mathematical learning at school and at home.
Teachers can allocate activities appropriate to classes, groups and individual learners and use information from the programme alongside their wider assessment.
How We Know Children Are Learning
Teachers continually check understanding through questioning, observation, discussion and children's independent work.
Children's ability to apply knowledge through fluency, reasoning and problem solving provides important evidence of how securely they understand a concept.
Cold and Hot Tasks, times-table assessment and ongoing classroom assessment help teachers identify progress, misconceptions and gaps in learning, informing what needs to be taught, revisited or practised next.
Science
Our Vision
We want children to be curious about the world around them and develop the scientific knowledge and thinking they need to understand and question it.
What Learning Looks Like
Our science curriculum progressively develops children's knowledge within biology, chemistry and physics, alongside their understanding of how scientists investigate the world.
Children learn to work scientifically by asking questions, observing, comparing, classifying, measuring, planning and undertaking investigations, recording results, interpreting evidence and drawing conclusions at an age-appropriate level.
Practical science provides purposeful opportunities to explore concepts and apply scientific knowledge rather than being an activity separate from learning.
Switched on Science is one of the resources used to support the planning and delivery of our science curriculum.
How We Know Children Are Learning
Teachers assess both children's scientific knowledge and their ability to work scientifically.
Evidence comes from discussion, questioning, assessments, children's written and practical work, investigations and opportunities to retrieve and apply previously learned scientific knowledge
History
Our Vision
We want children to develop a curiosity about the past and understand how people, events and societies have shaped the world in which they live.
What Learning Looks Like
Children progressively develop knowledge of British, local and wider world history.
Alongside historical knowledge, children learn to think historically by exploring:
Chronology | Cause and consequence | Change and continuity | Similarity and difference | Significance | Evidence
Children encounter historical sources, ask questions and consider how historians use evidence to develop interpretations of the past.
Rising Stars History is one of the principal resources supporting the sequencing and delivery of our history curriculum, with an emphasis on historical enquiry, knowledge, concepts and vocabulary.
How We Know Children Are Learning
Teachers assess children's ability to remember and connect important historical knowledge, use appropriate vocabulary and apply historical thinking.
Discussion, questioning, children's work and opportunities to retrieve previous learning help teachers establish how securely knowledge has been retained.
Geography
Our Vision
We want children to develop a lasting curiosity and fascination about the world, its people, places and environments.
What Learning Looks Like
Children progressively develop knowledge of their locality, the United Kingdom and the wider world, alongside an understanding of important human and physical geographical processes.
They learn to use geographical tools and methods including maps, atlases, globes, data and fieldwork.
Learning expands children's understanding from the local to the global, while geographical enquiry encourages them to ask questions about places, environments and the relationships between people and the world around them.
Rising Stars Geography is one of the resources supporting our curriculum, including geographical enquiry and the development of subject knowledge, concepts and vocabulary.
How We Know Children Are Learning
Teachers assess children's developing geographical knowledge, vocabulary and ability to apply geographical skills through discussion, written work, map work, fieldwork and opportunities to retrieve and connect previous learning.
Art & Design
Our Vision
We want children to develop the knowledge, skills, confidence and creativity to express ideas through art and appreciate the work of artists from different traditions, periods and cultures.
What Learning Looks Like
Children progressively develop artistic knowledge and techniques through experiences including drawing, painting, sculpture and other media.

Home Learning & Online Resources
Learning doesn't stop at the classroom door.
At Norbury Manor Primary School, we encourage children to continue exploring, practising and enjoying their learning at home. This page brings together our online learning platforms, information about our Dip and Do approach to home learning, and useful resources for families.
Children are encouraged to read regularly, practise key skills and take advantage of the learning opportunities available through our online platforms.
Our Online Learning Platforms

At Norbury Manor, our Dip and Do approach gives children opportunities to explore their learning beyond the classroom in creative and enjoyable ways.

There is no single way to complete a Dip and Do activity. Children might bring in a model, photograph, drawing, piece of writing, presentation or something completely different. We want children to take pride in their ideas and increasingly take responsibility for their own learning.
